item.title: ‘Weeks, not days’ in Kompany recovery, say Bayern
item.description: Bayern Munich expect coach Vincent Kompany to miss an extended period as he continues his hospital treatment for a virus after collapsing on the training pitch on Friday. Speaking at a press conference on Saturday, Bayern sporting director Max Eberl confirmed Kompany was still hospitalised in a “stable” condition. Kompany’s English assistant coach Aaron Danks will replace the 40-year-old for Sunday’s Bundesliga match at Freiburg. Eberl told reporters “examinations were continuing” to determine the nature of the former Manchester City and Belgium captain’s condition, with a recovery timeframe yet to be determined. “Vinnie will be given all the time he needs. We’re not starting to put together any timeframes. “We need to firstly figure out what it is and then we’ll discuss calmly what recovery time is to be. We won’t be talking about days, but weeks. We need to all be clear on that.” Taking Saturday’s press conference in Kompany’s absence, Danks said he had spoken with the former centre-back briefly on Friday but only to wish him well. “I explained to him that we wouldn’t be having no football conversations. It was just checking in on his health and making sure he’s OK. “All the football operations are in our hands and we’ll work together as a team to keep the club moving forward.” Bayern’s second team’s game was postponed yesterday after Kompany’s collapse but Eberl said the club did not consider trying to postpone Sunday’s Bundesliga game. “I think the greatest joy for Vinnie would be for us to play well tomorrow and, ideally, get a positive result,” Eberl said. “That would probably be one of the best things we could do to help him recover.” Danks confirmed Germany captain Joshua Kimmich, who has been on bereavement leave since Tuesday, would also miss Sunday’s game. Kompany returned to the dugout for Wednesday’s home clash with Arsenal despite missing the pre-match press conference due to the virus. Speaking after the Arsenal game, Kompany said his body reacted after he tried to push through the illness. “I caught a pretty nasty virus last week, and of course I didn’t listen to my body — and then at some point my body just said, ‘enough is enough!'” The defending champions sit on top of the Bundesliga table ahead of Sunday’s game, one point above Freiburg. Their next Champions League match is on November 3 in Madrid against Atletico. The post ‘Weeks, not days’ in Kompany recovery, say Bayern appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: North Korea’s Kim calls for training world’s ‘strongest’ military
item.description: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un urged his military to train to become the strongest in the world at a two-day meeting of company commanders in Pyongyang, state media said Saturday. Kim’s call for what he dubbed a “Korean-style military revolution” came the same week Seoul’s military proposed talks to clarify the border after an explosion inside the heavily fortified Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) further strained inter-Korean ties. Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war as the 1950-53 Korean War ended in a truce, not a peace treaty. The Pyongyang event, held Thursday and Friday, was aimed at developing a plan “to train the strongest armed forces in the world,” Kim said, according to the official Korea Central News Agency (KCNA). He also called for “all the companies” of the North’s army to be “turned into a strong elite unit in military and technical aspects and consolidated into perfect combat forces”. KCNA said it was the first gathering of “the entire army” since a February party congress where Kim had called for stronger conventional forces and reaffirmed plans to develop nuclear weapons and missiles. North Korea has also tested a slew of weapons recently, including a “new-type” precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which were said to use AI technology. Despite long-running UN sanctions, North Korea has enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state in law, with its regime repeatedly declaring its atomic arsenal permanent and irreversible. The North has also become a key Russian ally since it launched its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, sending troops to support Moscow’s war effort in return for economic benefits and military technology. South Korea proposed on Friday military talks with North Korea to clarify their border and restore communication channels, after Seoul blamed the DMZ blast that injured South Korean soldiers on North Korean landmines, a claim Pyongyang strongly rejected. Pyongyang, which also previously rejected Seoul’s demand for an apology over the explosion, has not responded to Friday’s proposal. c The post North Korea’s Kim calls for training world’s ‘strongest’ military appeared first on Vanguard News .

Sonny Areh, his media assistant, had also posted, on his facebook page, a birthday message to Dr Emmanuel Uduaghan, the immediate past governor of Delta State. He turned 62 last Saturday. What followed was an avalanche of birthday and goodwill messages. There were some in the newspapers too. And so the goodwill that marked Uduaghan’s two tenures as governor is still on the high. And people showed this at a thanksgiving service at the Guiding Light Assembly Church at Parkview Estate, Ikoyi, Lagos, last Sunday. Uduaghan was at the church to thank God for His mercies all these years. People turned out in numbers in the church where the pastor preached about the Holy Spirit. The word of God was good. And the people reveled in it. As the service was about to end, the pastor invited Uduaghan to make a brief remark after the church had prayed for him and his family. When he was done, the pastor prayed that more good things would continue to follow him. Uduaghan recalled one moment, as Governor of Delta State when he was caught between life and death and God saved his life. Part of his testimony went thus: “There are two things associated with governance. I call them the two Ps. They are Power and Pain. You see a governor and you marvel at the power he commands. He can order the arrest of somebody, he moves in a convoy, he has so much power that he earns tremendous respect everywhere. People see the glamour and the glitz, etc. But they don’t see the pain. There’s pain in governance. You can only rely on the grace of God to guide and guard you. ”When I came in as governor in 2007, the violence we battled then in Delta was more than what is happening now with the Avengers, etc. Kidnapping was high and expatriates were leaving. Militancy was more than what we have now. President Yar’Adua called me and said ‘what’s going on? These things are happening in your state.’ I told him that there were kaytwo ways to handle the militancy in Niger Delta. I asked that the Federal Government should do their own and I would do my own. We set out to work. I had to go to the creeks. We had to dialogue with these people. ”I remember one Sunday, my family and I had prepared to go to church and I received a call that they were going to burn Chevron terminal. The facility they planned to burn was so huge the impact would have been terrible for our oil production. I told them I would come after church service but they insisted I should come immediately otherwise the militants would destroy the terminal. I had to leave. I told my family to pray for me at the church. It was just one of my trips to the creeks. I took helicopter and then did the final journey by boat. And you know that when you go on such trips to the creeks you don’t take escorts or when you take them they don’t carry guns. I went with only my ADC. No guns. It was a huge risk but one that I had to take to engage them and stop the blowing up of the oil facilities. ”It was a terrible place. I got to the place and after discussing with the militants they told me that there were higher authorities further inside that I must meet and that what I had just done was a preliminary one. They were all armed to the teeth, fierce-looking and ready to pull the trigger. You could imagine how dangerous it was in that terrain. I continued the journey further into the creeks to meet their superiors. I got there and they led me into a room. They were kind enough to offer me a seat. With their guns, some pointing at me, they sat on the floor while we held talks on why they should spare the oil facility. I spent hours with the them. I finished with them and left for the journey back home. ”While on the boat going back, we noticed one speed boat racing to where we were. They caught up with us. We didn’t know if it was another group but they caught up with us and one of them pointed his AK 47 at me and put his finger at the trigger. It was terrifying. It was a moment of life or death within seconds. You could see the anger on the face of the militant, who pointed the gun at me. He wanted to shoot. It was terrifying. There was nothing I could do but to pray silently. I was praying. Silently, I prayed and I waved the white handkerchief (peace signal) I had. The man steadied the gun at me. Suddenly another speed boat from nowhere dashed in between and and after some seconds they all sped off. ‘I believe that The Holy Spirit appeared in that white handkerchief and saved my life and I live today to give this testimony. ”There were other terrible encounters one had as governor but people would not know about these pains. What they know is the glamour or power they associate with you in governance. I thank God for what he had done for a village man like me. I come from a village setting where there were no roads, no electricity, no facilities, just village life – our parents were farming and fishing for us to go to school. I remember when I eventually had a Beetle car and how my wife prayed for us to have a better car, a better air conditioned car possibly a Mercedez Benz. And she used to sing a song about this. It also invites a necessary public question: what happens after the judge has spoken? Does the order translate into actual release? Have all those covered by the ruling been accounted for? If implementation is delayed or disputed, what explanation is provided, and what lawful remedies remain available? Vanguard source confirmed that the Court orders were validly served on the military authorities. The source stated that a powerful delegation of Four Traditional Rulers and some top military brass of Urhobo nation visited the Minister of Defence, but nothing tangible is yet to be achieved. When silence becomes another question Okuama’s anguish extends beyond detention Reports emerged in December 2024 that community President-General James Oghoroko had died in military custody while treasurer Dennis Okugbaye was reported terribly sick and was later released. The military announced that an investigation into the reported deaths had been ordered. The death added another grave dimension to a story already marked by loss and uncertainty. What did the investigations establish? Were the circumstances fully documented? Were the families given clear answers? What findings, if any, have since been made public? These questions should not be answered by assumption, political convenience or rumour. They demand verifiable evidence and transparent communication from the appropriate authorities. Silence, by itself, proves neither guilt nor innocence. But where serious questions concern human lives and the conduct of public institutions, sustained uncertainty can deepen public mistrust. The answer is not louder accusation. It is credible information, lawful accountability and a process that people can examine. Who carries the responsibility? A court does not ordinarily enforce its decisions through words alone. The implementation of its orders depends on the relevant institutions and the procedures established by law. That is why the Okuama story cannot end with the announcement of a judgment. The relevant authorities must clarify the implementation status of the release order. Outstanding questions surrounding the reported death in custody require clear, evidence-based answers. The rights of affected persons must be respected, while the deaths of the 17 military personnel must remain part of the broader pursuit of accountability. These responsibilities do not cancel one another out. Demanding due process for detained community leaders does not diminish the lives of the slain military personnel. Seeking answers about custody conditions does not prejudge the outcome of an investigation. Insisting on lawful enforcement of a court order does not place anyone above the law. Rather, these demands point towards a common principle: justice must be measured by established facts, fair procedures and the faithful application of the law. The danger of an unfinished ending There is a particular sadness in stories that become quieter as the questions grow more difficult. A headline appears. Public attention rises. Officials make statements. A court issues a decision. Then the national conversation shifts, and focus moves elsewhere. But the families do not move on at the same speed as the news cycle. The consequences of detention, loss, and community displacement do not disappear when public attention fades. For Okuama, the danger is that an extraordinary sequence of events may gradually become an ordinary footnote in the nation’s political history. That would leave the most important questions suspended between what has been announced and what has been independently established. The community does not need another cycle of recrimination. It needs clarity about the status of its leaders, credible answers to outstanding questions and a path towards recovery that acknowledges the suffering of everyone affected. The final question Perhaps the real test of justice begins after the courtroom empties. When the judge has delivered a ruling and the record has been closed for the day, who ensures that the decision is implemented? Who explains delays, if any? Who provides families with reliable information? Who follows through when an investigation is announced? And who remains answerable when public attention turns elsewhere? These are not questions for the courtroom alone. They concern the institutions, procedures and public responsibilities upon which the rule of law depends. Okuama’s story remains a reminder that a judicial pronouncement can mark a turning point without necessarily resolving every question surrounding a crisis. The court may speak. The law may provide the answers. But the public must still be able to establish what happened next. For in the end, justice is not measured only by the words delivered from the bench, but also by the lawful actions that follow. And so, as Okuama waits for clarity on the questions that remain, one question continues to echo beyond the courtroom walls: When the court speaks, who answers — and who ensures that the answer becomes reality? item.description: President Bola Tinubu will formally open his re-election campaign in Kaduna on Saturday. The location is deliberate, the arithmetic is formidable, and the message is unmistakable: the All Progressives Congress intends to win the 2027 election by rebuilding a northern coalition around the President. The three northern geopolitical zones contain 56.01 million of Nigeria’s 103.43 million registered voters; 54.2 per cent of the national register. The North-West alone has 25.08 million, making it the country’s largest electoral bloc. APC campaign officials are consequently talking about northern consensus and setting a national target of approximately 40 million votes. But registered voters are not actual votes, political endorsements are not public opinion, and the North is not a single electoral personality. That is the political signal this week. The party’s challenge is that political machinery can mobilise supporters, but it cannot permanently insulate an incumbent from lived economic experience. The contest between structure and hardship The APC’s campaign argument will be that the most painful period of reform has passed. Inflation has moderated, foreign reserves have improved, economic growth has strengthened, and the Central Bank has begun adjusting interest rates. The administration will argue that removing the petrol subsidy and reforming the foreign-exchange market prevented a deeper fiscal crisis. The opposition’s reply is more immediate: food, transport, energy and business costs remain painfully high. That explains the political significance of the National Economic Council’s newly approved 90-day action plan. It prioritises food affordability, tax harmonisation, completion of high-impact projects, removal of investment bottlenecks and regulated household support. It also proposes a national dashboard to track projects and the use of savings from subsidy removal. On paper, these are reasonable interventions. The problem is timing. The presidential election is 86 days away, while the relief plan is designed to run for 90 days. Atiku’s campaign has therefore called it “election bait,” arguing that Nigerians are being asked to vote before the promised relief can be fully assessed. That is a partisan allegation, not proof that the programme is improper. But the calendar gives the criticism political force. The government can answer it only through early, measurable delivery. What food has become cheaper? Which households have received support? What projects have been completed? How much has been spent, by whom and under what criteria? Announcements will not be sufficient. The electorate needs receipts. The opposition’s unity problem While the APC prepares a major campaign launch, opposition parties are again discussing a consensus candidate. Representatives of the ADC, NDC, PRP, SDP, APM and PDP have inaugurated legal and media committees to develop a framework for cooperation. Atiku, Peter Obi, Donald Duke and Adewale Adebayo are among the names mentioned in the talks. Coalition organisers say negotiations are progressing towards a single candidate. That claim should be treated cautiously. The Independent National Electoral Commission has already published 18 presidential candidates, including Atiku for the ADC and Obi for the NDC. Agreeing that the opposition should unite is therefore much easier than determining who withdraws, who leads, what happens to the running mates and how supporters are transferred between parties. There is also no guarantee that voters will follow elite instructions. An Atiku endorsement of Obi would not automatically deliver Atiku’s northern vote. An Obi endorsement of Atiku would not automatically transfer younger urban voters or the South-East. Nigerian politicians often mistake negotiations among leaders for consolidation among electorates. The opposition nevertheless understands the arithmetic. Tinubu won in 2023 with 36.61 per cent of the valid votes; 8.79 million votes. Atiku and Obi together received more than 13 million. That does not mean a joint ticket would have automatically defeated Tinubu, because elections are shaped by turnout, geography and the constitutional requirement for national spread. But it shows why fragmentation remains the APC’s quiet ally. Unless the coalition produces a credible agreement quickly, it risks becoming a committee for managing defeat. The allegation does not establish manipulation. Technical delays or publication problems are not evidence of a compromised register. But INEC should resolve the issue immediately. A national figure cannot substitute for a register that citizens and parties can scrutinise. The public must be able to identify duplicate entries, deceased persons, omissions and questionable registrations before the final roll is certified. item.title: Mourinho must stop Barca machine as Clasico tensions resume
item.description: Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho will renew one of football’s most bitter rivalries on Sunday when he takes charge of his first Clasico since returning to the club, with La Liga leaders Barcelona awaiting him at Camp Nou. The Portuguese veteran’s first spell at Madrid was defined in large part by his battle to end Barca’s dominance under Pep Guardiola, with relations between the Spanish giants slumping to their lowest ebb. item.title: Ebola vaccine trial begins in DR Congo
item.description: The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo began Friday, the head of the World Health Organization said. The DR Congo’s worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,700-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,600. Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic. Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will be put through a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo. The trial began with the first shot of Ervebo being administered in Bunia, the capital of the DRC’s northeastern Ituri province, which is the epicentre of the outbreak. “Science gives us hope. Today, in Bunia DRC, the first participants were vaccinated in a new Ebola vaccine trial called Tumaini, which means ‘hope’ in Swahili,” WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X. “This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work,” he said, adding that in the meantime, the existing Ervebo vaccine would be tested. “WHO is supporting this DRC-led effort to find answers and save lives.” – Two vaccines in the pipeline – The so-called Tumaini trial is a single trial framework that can test the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity of multiple vaccines. The trial will use a ring vaccination approach: immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection. It is gearing up to incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are currently advancing through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials. One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the US-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology. item.title: Tinubu appointed Muri-Okunola because of Gbajabiamila’s failure — Laolu Akande
item.description: Former presidential aide, Laolu Akande, has attributed President Bola Tinubu’s decision to bring Hakeem Muri-Okunola into the Presidency to what he described as the failure of Chief of Staff Femi Gbajabiamila to perform his duties effectively. Akande said the president’s reliance on Muri-Okunola, his Principal Private Secretary, to organise his schedule suggested shortcomings in the management of the Presidency. Speaking on the Naija Unfiltered Podcast, Akande argued that Tinubu had failed to surround himself with influential and capable figures who could help him deliver effective governance. He said Muri-Okunola, a former Lagos State Head of Service, had been brought in to organise the president’s schedule despite the presence of a chief of staff. “This is the problem. The president has a chief of staff, for instance, even the people in that Villa will tell you that the chief in front of the staff is removed because of all the kinds of stuff that have happened and then the president has to go and bring Hakeem Muri-Okunola (HMO) to be organising his schedule,” Akande said. He argued that the need for Muri-Okunola’s involvement pointed to a failure by the chief of staff to carry out his responsibilities. “If the chief of staff was doing his job properly, he wouldn’t need HMO; that’s the truth,” he said. Akande, who served as Senior Media Aide to former Vice President Yemi Osinbajo under the late President Muhammadu Buhari, said Tinubu had yet to deliver his best in office despite having some capable people in his administration. “So, the president has not managed to give us his best, and there are very good people in this administration. There are good people, few people, but they don’t have that kind of influence that people like Fashola, Osinbajo, Aregbesola, Cardoso,” he said. He cited former Lagos State Governor Babatunde Fashola, Osinbajo, former Osun State Governor Rauf Aregbesola and Central Bank of Nigeria Governor Olayemi Cardoso as examples of people with the experience and influence he believes Tinubu needs around him. Akande also praised Cardoso’s performance at the apex bank, saying the president appeared to give him room to work because of their familiarity. “The president even doesn’t try to interfere with Cardoso because he knows him. I think they call him Head Master or whatever. He looks everything. The president doesn’t have people like that around him,” he said. Muri-Okunola previously served as Lagos State Head of Service before becoming Tinubu’s Principal Private Secretary at the Presidency. item.title: Iran says US military not allowed to enter Gulf ‘under any circumstances’
item.description: Iran said on Saturday that US military ships would never be allowed to enter the Gulf “under any circumstances” and President Donald Trump will “take that dream to his grave”. The remarks came amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as US ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack warned that Washington could “absolutely” strike Iran as soon as this weekened. “We will not allow US military ships in the Persian Gulf under any circumstances and at any time,” said Iran’s armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, according to Iranian state television. “The US president must dream of seeing the armed forces enter the Persian Gulf. He will take that dream to his grave.” Iranian forces have restricted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy conduit and gateway to the Gulf, since the war with the United States broke out on February 28. In retaliation, the United States has imposed a counterblockade on Iranian ports and ships. Tehran has required vessels to seek permission to transit, and repeatedly targeted ships attempting to pass through Hormuz via a southern route close to the Omani coast. According to the Guards, several tankers attempting to transit Hormuz through the route Tehran considers “illegal” were hit by mines in recent days. On Friday, the Guards said two supertankers carrying more than 4.5 million barrels of crude oil have been abandoned at sea after hitting mines in the strategic waterway. “Their engine rooms were disabled by an explosion and a fierce fire,” the Guards said in a statement carried by their Sepah News website. item.title: Why some people in Tinubu’s govt don’t want Fashola around – Laolu Akande
item.description: Former presidential aide, Laolu Akande, has alleged that some people around President Bola Tinubu do not want former Minister of Works and Housing, Babatunde Fashola, in the current administration because he would not tolerate certain practices within the government. Akande said Fashola’s absence from the government could partly be due to fatigue but argued that the opposition of some people around Tinubu was a more significant factor. He spoke during an interview on the Naija Unfiltered Podcast, where he also discussed Tinubu’s government and the perceived fallout between the president and former Vice President Yemi Osinbajo. Akande, who served as Senior Media Aide to Osinbajo under former President Muhammadu Buhari, described Fashola as someone who would not compromise his principles to accommodate those around him. “I think the reason why Fashola is not in this government, two reasons. I think Fashola himself has a bit of fatigue, more importantly, I think there are people around the president who don’t want to see Fashola because Fashola is not going to tolerate many of those things that you are seeing around,” he said. Akande added that Fashola was known for standing his ground, suggesting that his disposition might have made some people in the president’s circle uncomfortable. “Whatever you say about Fashola, he doesn’t take nonsense and the people who wanted to get some nonsense going, they didn’t want Fashola,” he said. The former presidential aide, however, said Fashola remained close to Tinubu and had not had a major public disagreement with the president. He suggested that, despite the absence of an open confrontation, there could be underlying tensions between the two politicians. “Even somebody like Fashola, who is still very close to the president — no problems openly, although they are also under current which he will speak about, but at least he didn’t have any blowout problem with the man,” Akande said. He maintained that some people around Tinubu did not want individuals like Fashola in the administration for reasons beyond the former minister’s own reluctance to return to government. item.title: Uyo remains home ground for Super Eagles for now
item.description: The Nigeria Football Federation is not ready to move the Super Eagles’ home games from Uyo to Lagos, with a senior official saying Lagos is under consideration but Uyo stays the venue for now. The comments followed the Super Eagles’ 3-0 loss to Guinea-Bissau in an AFCON 2027 qualifier. Nigeria have three points from two Group L games, while Guinea-Bissau lead the group on six, the outlet said. It was earlier reported that the Super Eagles could host November qualifiers in Lagos. But the renovated Teslim Balogun Stadium is not yet ready to host an international. NFF inspectors will visit once the Lagos State Government finishes the renovation. The federation is also considering friendlies at Teslim Balogun to test the facilities and gauge the reaction of fans, and plans to consult players before deciding, the report said. The official argued that changing a settled home ground could hurt performance. The Super Eagles have played most of their home games in Uyo for nearly a decade. The NFF’s stated reasoning is cautious, and the logic is easy to follow: a stadium that has not been inspected cannot host a qualifier. The harder question is the calendar. With less than a month to the November double-header against Tanzania, there is little room for inspections and approvals if Lagos were chosen. If the stadium is not signed off in time, Uyo is the only practical option for the next home game, whatever the appetite for change. If it is, the NFF has said it would test the venue with a friendly first, which suggests a move for a competitive match would come later rather than sooner. April was brutal and beautiful. 100 Bundesliga goals in record time, then that semi-final vs PSG where he scored twice but Bayern went out 6-5 on aggregate. At the World Cup he led England to bronze with 6 goals, including a 6-4 thriller against France in the third-place playoff. Could he be the first English winner since Michael Owen in 2001? Then Kylian Mbappe – football’s ultimate World Cup man. 38 goals in 33 games for Real Madrid before the tournament, winning the Pichichi. Then in America, 10 goals to become the World Cup’s all-time top scorer at just 27. He is now the first player in history to win the Golden Boot in the Champions League, La Liga and the World Cup in the same calendar year – a treble of scoring crowns that may never be broken. His moment was not lifting the trophy – France finished fourth – but the way he left it all on the pitch. A breathtaking opener against Senegal to get his World Cup account going, a hat-trick vs Norway in the group stage, and four assists on top of the 10 goals. 22 goals in 22 games across three World Cups is the story of greatness. He did not win the World Cup, but he won history. Lamine Yamal is so many people’s favourite. He and Olise at the highest level are the most entertaining footballers in the game at the moment and he already has an archive of breathtaking goals. At 19, he could become the youngest Ballon d’Or winner ever, a record held by the great Ronaldo Nazario who won it at 21 years and 96 days in 1997. Yamal’s story writes itself: La Liga champion, La Liga Player of the Year, and then World Champion with Spain. His tournament was quiet by his standards, but he contributed to Spain’s victory which was largely a team performance. He completed 27 dribbles from 51 attempts – the highest total at the World Cup. He was Man of the Match twice, against Austria and Belgium in the semi-final – a game in which Spain were underdogs – and he won the crucial penalty that gave Spain the opening goal. For Barcelona this past season: 24 goals and 17 assists, averaging a goal contribution every 85 minutes. He is no longer the future. He is the present. If Yamal is the present, Michael Olise is pure magic. Bundesliga Player of the Season with numbers that read like a video game – 15 goals, 19 assists in the league, 22 goals and 31 assists in 52 games across all competitions. Two moments define him. First, the Freiburg game: Bayern down 0-2, Olise scores two and assists three in a 6-2 comeback. Then the quarter-final vs Real Madrid – 90+3, 4-3 on the night, that left-foot curler past Lunin to send Bayern through. At the World Cup he broke Pelé’s record with 7 assists in one tournament for France. As Thomas Müller said, “He has that dance-like, artistic ease you can’t learn.” And then Lionel Messi. At 39, in what might be his last World Cup, he took Argentina to the final and lost 1-0 to Spain in extra time. Heartbreak in New Jersey. He was Player of the Tournament until the final against Spain. He single-handedly dragged Argentina to the World Cup final in a manner that clearly stood him apart from the pack. But look at what he still did: 25 goals and 15 assists for Inter Miami this season, first player ever to record 15+ assists in three straight MLS seasons, first to have 30+ goal contributions in three different seasons. His moment? October 17th vs Atlanta – two goals, one assist, his 934th career goal. He is chasing a third straight MLS MVP. He is 39 and still top-two in the Golden Boot race. The defending champion Ousmane Dembele wants back-to-back. PSG retained both Ligue 1 and the Champions League, and Dembele was again their engine – 20 goals in the league campaign, 7 in the Champions League. His best moment came in the World Cup quarter-final run – 6 goals including that hat-trick against Norway. France faded late, but Dembele proved last year’s Ballon d’Or was no fluke. Can he retain it? Rodri is the anomaly. He left Manchester City for Barcelona this summer after winning the World Cup Golden Ball. Spain’s captain, the metronome who made Spain champions again. His moment wasn’t a goal, it was control. In the final against Argentina, with Messi throwing everything at Spain in extra time, Rodri won the ball back 11 times and completed 96% of his passes. The anchor. The man who makes everyone else look good. So who does the cap fit? If you want pure numbers, it’s Kane. If you want trophies, it’s Yamal. If you want history, it’s Mbappe. If you want beauty, it’s Olise. If you want longevity, it’s Messi. If it was just about who was the best player at the World Cup, Rodri has a real shout – World Cup winner and Golden Ball winner. On October 26th at the London Palladium, football will finally have to choose. For once, there is no wrong answer – only a hard one. item.title: Emmanuel Uduaghan: My boss sleeps
item.description: By Sunny Areh Delta weeps today. The stethoscope that once listened to the heartbeat of our state is still. His Excellency, Dr. Emmanuel Eweta Uduaghan, has gone home, two sunrises shy of 72. You governed with a smile, you led with a listening heart. This morning of October 19, 2026, that smile rests. You did not rule us, you treated us. You diagnosed our pains, you prescribed progress, you built with the patience of a physician. You dreamed of a Delta Beyond Oil because you believed in a people beyond riches. I have lost my boss, my teacher, my light. Rest well, Your Excellency. Your memory will forever remain in our hearts, and your legacy will endure in the lives of those you touched. Go well, Dr. Emmanuel Eweta Uduaghan, Physician of Delta, Father to many, Boss to me. Your light never dies. May your gentle soul rest in perfect peace. This is an immeasurably sad day for me By Tony Nwaka What can I say? How do I begin to narrate my story with him? Will words ever be enough to capture the breadth of his affection towards me? How can I ever forget those exceptionally inspiring words he said to me some days after he was elected Governor of Delta State in 2007? I had gone to meet him at his residence with my CV. As he saw me clutching the big brown envelope, he asked, “What is that you have in your hand?” “I have come to present my CV to you, sir, so you could kindly consider me for a position in your government,” I said in a smattering, somewhat quivering tone. He looked at me from head to toe, smiled, and as he walked away, said, “Return your CV, I don’t need it. People who intend to work with me should rather be bringing their CVs to you for onward submission to me.” I was stunned and speechless as I returned home that day with my CV, bristling with overwhelming wonder and inexpressible gratitude. And as a man of his word, he not only appointed me as a commissioner in his government, he kept me for the entire eight-year duration of his tenure. That is the man who has just exited the portals of mortality. Indeed, a great man is gone. I have lost a beloved political father — Dr. Emmanuel Eweta Uduaghan, Governor of Delta State (2007-2015). My heartfelt condolences to Her Excellency, Mrs. Roli Uduaghan, and the entire Uduaghan family. I pray his soul finds eternal repose with the Lord, and may His inexhaustible beneficence grant his family the fortitude to bear the loss. item.title: Ebola Vaccine Trial Begins In DR Congo – WHO Chief
item.description: The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo began Friday, the head of the World Health Organization said. The DR Congo’s worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,700-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,600. Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic.
